3Battery Materials Lab.
 Composition-dependent porosity in five simulated beds
• Soft-sphere DEM with a linear hysteretic contact law, pressed to 300 MPa; one bed per 
composition, no seed replicates.
• One 7:3 bed: porosity 31.8 → 25.1 → 16.7 → 16.5 % (final state relaxed at fixed platen); 7:3 
(large : small NCM) is the lowest of the five beds.

4Battery Materials Lab.
 From the contact network to Li⁺ transport
• Contact-network approach [8]: bulk resistance + Holm/Maxwell constriction using Hertz 
contact radii; chosen σ₀ = 1.5 mS cm⁻¹ (pellet-literature range).
• Transport tortuosity T = φ_SE σ₀ / σ_eff: 7.2 → 5.0 (0:10 → 7:3). Contact constriction accounts 
for 73–75 % of Joule dissipation in this network model.

5Battery Materials Lab.
 Fixed-shape DEM limits and the material point method (MPM)
• No shape change and no yield cap: overlap is the only plasticity proxy; the softened SE 
modulus (1.35 vs ≈ 22 GPa) is an effective parameter, not a property [1, 7].
• J2 plasticity on a background grid: shape change and void filling that a fixed-shape sphere 
cannot represent; active material is kept rigid (DEM skeleton), only the electrolyte flows.

• Bulk modulus from DFT; shear softening and yield stress from a pure-electrolyte calibration

7Battery Materials Lab.
 Voxelizing the compacted microstructure into a transport mesh
• Faces are joined by a harmonic mean with no interface-resistance term: an ideal-interface 
voxel model — an upper bound only within the same geometry, properties and boundaries.
• VGCF as diameter-preserving segments, PTFE as a centre-line insulator, polymer as spheres; a 
registered 104-arm study keeps the σ(e⁻) order across 1–4 wt% VGCF on all tested grids 
(72/72).
Transport

8Battery Materials Lab.
 Problems 1 and 2: grid dependence and absolute σ(e⁻)
• The electronic ratio decreases across the three tested voxel spacings (0.4, 0.3, 0.25 µm); the 
ionic ratio crosses 1. Grid convergence has not been established.
• Voxel predictions exceed the available DC-polarization estimates; measurement conditions 
remain unverified. The NCM–SE comparison uses a common reference conductivity and a 
specified contact model.
Limits
This work — voxel transport solver (a, b) · contact network, five NCM–SE beds (c)
(a) same bed pair and convention; no converged conductivity ratio is reported · (b) log scale; conditions not yet matched ·
(c) no carbon/binder; Hertz H0; common NCM reference 4.1 mS cm⁻¹ [16]; size factor off; one bed per composition

9Battery Materials Lab.
 Problem 3: Load sharing during compaction
• NCM–NCM contacts contribute 48–60 % of vertical stress after relaxation at fixed platen 
position; 7:3 is the minimum.
• The porosity ranking agrees for the selected five compositions (exploratory comparison, n = 5).

11Battery Materials Lab.
 Drum mixing of a layered NCM–SE bed: no segregation detected
• Rotating-drum DEM with a cohesive soft-contact model: ten runs from a layered initial state, 
eight revolutions; Lacey index M on a 16×16×4 bin grid vs a random reference.
• No NCM–NCM cohesion vs reference cohesion: ΔM within seed-to-seed scatter = the 
registered "no segregation" category (not "no effect"), direction and size unresolved.
Mixing
This work (left) · figure: presenter — bed view, layered start and after eight revolutions (right)
M = 1: fully mixed; error bars = within-run SD; all ten runs reach M ≈ 
0.96–1.00, so this bin grid cannot separate the arms;
the registered 1 % overlap condition of the contact model was not 
met (diagnostic)

12Battery Materials Lab.
 Cohesion exploration: stronger cohesion lowers mixing
• Exploratory single-seed runs, two revolutions: NCM–NCM cohesion raised 10× and 30×, or all 
contact pairs raised 10× and 14×, vs the run without NCM–NCM cohesion.
• ΔM grows with the Bond number in every bin grid, but each arm is one seed chosen after 
earlier runs, and wall adhesion changes with the pair — no verdict is drawn.
Mixing
This work (left) · figure: presenter — bed snapshots, non-cohesive vs cohesive NCM, two revolutions (right)
hatched: bin grid failed the volume-coverage check; ΔM mixes the 
start-state difference

13Battery Materials Lab.
 Surface energy and coating: SE–SE adhesion is the open term
• Two NCM–SE contacts → NCM–NCM + SE–SE frees ΔW = 2(√γ_A − √γ_S)² ≥ 0; the small SE 
phase keeps like–like contacts best, so uncoated beds can retain SE–SE clusters.
• Uniformly cohesive runs keep most SE in SE–SE clusters after two revolutions, unlike the run 
without NCM–NCM cohesion; the confirmatory 18-run block stays on hold.

W = work of adhesion, R* = reduced radius, ρ = density of the smaller particle); the uncoated NCM / SE surface-energy ratio is not

14Battery Materials Lab.
Plan
 Tests for unresolved model limits
• Grid sensitivity remains unresolved. Diagnostic results exist, while final hypothesis verdicts 
remain pending.

contacts
Pending: separate launch approvals for the updated 194-bed run and the 20-bed extension.

15Battery Materials Lab.
Summary
 Current findings and limitations
• DEM and contact networks: composition trends from one bed per composition
• MPM: plastic deformation, with compaction agreement dependent on initialization and loading 
protocol
• Voxel transport: ideal-interface calculations with grid dependence and unresolved absolute 
conductivity
• Mixing: no segregation detected at the registered resolution; cohesion exploration without a 
verdict
• Final model-validation verdicts remain pending
